paragraphs.title: The Psalm’s Title and Longing for God

answers: The water brooks
The house of God
The enemy’s sword
easy.explanation: The verse says, “As the hart panteth after the water brooks.”
easy.q: What does the hart pant after?

answers: The multitude
God, the living God
The waterspouts
easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist’s soul thirst for?

answers: When shall I come and appear before God?
When shall I find the water brooks?
When shall I escape the multitude?
easy.explanation: He asks, “When shall I come and appear before God?”

answers: He compares it to a king’s desire for victory
He compares it to a hart’s thirst for water
He compares it to an enemy’s hunger for battle
medium.explanation: His longing for God is compared with the hart panting after water brooks.
medium.q: What comparison does the psalmist make about his longing for God?

answers: Longs or thirsts intensely
Speaks angrily
Sleeps peacefully
medium.explanation: “Panteth” describes an intense longing or thirst.
medium.q: What does the word “panteth” most nearly mean in this passage?

answers: Because he wants to appear before Him
Because he wants to hide from Him
Because he wants to lead the multitude
medium.explanation: He longs to “come and appear before God.”
medium.q: Why does the psalmist desire to come before God?

answers: It is casual and temporary
It is urgent and deeply necessary
It is mainly connected with earthly wealth
challenge.explanation: A thirsty hart urgently needs water, illustrating the psalmist’s deep need for God.
challenge.q: What does the image of the hart reveal about the psalmist’s desire for God?

answers: The psalmist is separated from God’s presence but longs to approach Him
The psalmist has already rejected God completely
The psalmist is celebrating a military victory
challenge.explanation: The question expresses separation, longing, and the desire to come before God.
challenge.q: What contrast is suggested by the question, “When shall I come and appear before God?”

answers: They move from physical thirst to spiritual thirst and longing for God
They move from war to political rule
They move from joy to confidence in human strength
challenge.explanation: The image of thirst develops into the soul’s intense longing for the living God.
challenge.q: How do the first three verses develop one central idea?

paragraphs.title: Exile and the Memory of Going to the House of God

answers: His tears
His praise
His victory
easy.explanation: He says, “My tears have been my meat day and night.”
easy.q: What had been the psalmist’s meat day and night?

answers: Where is thy house?
Where is thy God?
Where is thy multitude?
easy.explanation: They continually said, “Where is thy God?”
easy.q: What question did people continually ask the psalmist?

answers: To the house of God
To the battlefield
To the water brooks
easy.explanation: He remembers going with the multitude “to the house of God.”
easy.q: Where had the psalmist gone with the multitude?

answers: Constant sorrow and distress
Joyful celebration
Confidence in his enemies
medium.explanation: The continual tears show that the psalmist is suffering deeply.
medium.q: What do the psalmist’s tears day and night communicate?

answers: The voice of joy and praise
The sound of battle
Complete silence
medium.explanation: The procession included “the voice of joy and praise.”
medium.q: What characterized the multitude going to the house of God?

answers: It kept holyday
It fled from the enemy
It searched for water
medium.explanation: He remembers going with “a multitude that kept holyday.”
medium.q: What does the psalmist remember about the multitude?

answers: Present tears and mockery are contrasted with joyful worship remembered from the past
Physical hunger is contrasted with military success
Nighttime silence is contrasted with daytime labor
challenge.explanation: The psalmist suffers in the present but remembers joyful worship with the multitude.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in these verses?

answers: It reminds him of the worship and fellowship from which he is now separated
It proves that he no longer believes in God
It shows that the enemies have joined the multitude
challenge.explanation: The happy memory highlights his present distance from the house of God.
challenge.q: Why would remembering the joyful procession deepen the psalmist’s sorrow?

answers: It intensifies the psalmist’s emotional pain
It announces the beginning of a feast
It confirms that the psalmist has won a battle
challenge.explanation: The enemies’ reproach adds pressure and sorrow to his already painful condition.
challenge.q: What effect does the enemies’ question, “Where is thy God?” have in the passage?

answers: His soul
His enemies
The multitude
easy.explanation: The psalmist speaks directly to his own soul.
easy.q: To whom does the psalmist speak when he says, “Why art thou cast down”?

answers: Hope in God
Flee from the waters
Reproach the multitude
easy.explanation: He commands his soul, “hope thou in God.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist tell his soul to do?

answers: Deep, waterspouts, waves, and billows
Dew, mist, and gentle rain
A fountain, a brook, and a well
easy.q: What images appear in the description of the waters?

answers: A dejected or discouraged soul
A soul filled with victory
A soul preparing for a feast
medium.explanation: “Cast down” describes the psalmist’s discouraged emotional state.
medium.q: What does “cast down” describe in this passage?

answers: They picture the overwhelming troubles passing over him
They describe a peaceful celebration
They show that he has reached the house of God
medium.explanation: The powerful water imagery conveys the force of his troubles and inner turmoil.
medium.q: How do the waves and billows relate to the psalmist’s experience?

answers: Praise God
Escape to the mountains
Answer the enemies with a sword
medium.explanation: He says, “I shall yet praise him.”
medium.q: What does the psalmist say he will yet do?

answers: The psalmist is deeply distressed, yet he urges himself to hope in God
The psalmist is celebrating, yet he refuses to praise God
The psalmist is physically thirsty, yet he rejects all water
challenge.explanation: His distress is real, but he responds by directing his soul toward hope and praise.
challenge.q: What tension is present in these verses?

answers: It shows the psalmist actively fighting discouragement with faith
It proves that the psalmist has forgotten God
It shifts the subject from worship to military planning
challenge.explanation: The repeated command functions as self-encouragement in the midst of distress.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of repeating the command to hope in God?

answers: It makes the psalmist’s troubles seem powerful and overwhelming
It turns the passage into a description of ordinary travel
It suggests that the enemies have been defeated
challenge.explanation: The deep, waves, and billows vividly portray the intensity of his upheaval.
challenge.q: How does the water imagery strengthen the emotional meaning of the passage?

paragraphs.title: Kindness, Prayer, and the Plea for Salvation

answers: His lovingkindness
The enemy’s reproach
The waterspouts
easy.explanation: The verse says, “the LORD will command his lovingkindness in the daytime.”
easy.q: What will the LORD command in the daytime?

answers: The LORD’s song and his prayer
A multitude keeping holyday
The enemy’s sword
easy.explanation: At night, “his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life.”
easy.q: What will be with the psalmist in the night?

answers: My rock
My enemy
My multitude
easy.explanation: He says, “I will say unto God my rock.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist call God in his prayer?

answers: God’s lovingkindness is present by day, and a song and prayer remain at night
The enemies rule by day, and the multitude rules at night
The psalmist rejoices by day, but forgets God at night
medium.explanation: The passage presents divine kindness by day and continued worship through the night.
medium.q: What relationship between day and night is presented in the passage?

answers: He feels forgotten and oppressed by the enemy
He is angry that the multitude is celebrating
He cannot find the water brooks
medium.explanation: He asks, “Why hast thou forgotten me?” and mentions the oppression of the enemy.
medium.q: What complaint does the psalmist make to God?

answers: God is a source of strength and security
God is distant and powerless
God is merely part of the landscape
medium.explanation: Calling God “my rock” presents Him as a firm refuge and source of strength.
medium.q: What does the phrase “my rock” suggest about God?

answers: It moves from confidence in God’s kindness, through complaint, toward renewed hope and praise
It moves from celebration, through victory, toward rejection of God
It moves from physical thirst, through battle, toward political power
challenge.explanation: The psalmist recognizes God’s kindness, voices his pain, and still looks toward praise and salvation.
challenge.q: How does the passage progress emotionally?

answers: He still turns to God as his rock and source of life
He has abandoned all trust in God
He believes his enemies are stronger than God
challenge.explanation: Even while asking why he feels forgotten, he addresses God as “my rock” and “the God of my life.”
challenge.q: What does the psalmist’s prayer reveal despite his complaint?

answers: It returns to the psalmist’s repeated self-encouragement to expect God’s help and praise Him
It rejects the earlier longing for God’s presence
It changes the subject from spiritual trouble to farming
challenge.explanation: The ending repeats the call to hope and affirms that the psalmist will yet praise God for His help.
challenge.q: How does the closing command to hope in God connect with the earlier verses?
